name: Direct Prompt Injection
oneLine: Attacker-controlled instructions in the user turn override the agent’s goal and tool policy.
description: The original agentic hijack: a user or upstream system places imperative text in the prompt so the model abandons its system policy. Direct injection is the delivery mechanism for many later classes — tool misuse, privilege abuse, and exfiltration all start here when the model treats the turn as authority.

name: Indirect Prompt Injection
oneLine: Untrusted retrieved content — email, docs, web — hijacks a privileged agent with no user click.
description: The agent retrieves attacker-controlled text (mail, wiki, issue, webpage) into context and follows it as instruction. EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) was the first documented zero-click production case: a malicious email caused Microsoft 365 Copilot to exfiltrate mailbox data through a rendered image URL.

name: Tool Poisoning
oneLine: Hidden directives in MCP tool descriptions steer the model to steal secrets or call extra tools.
description: Tool metadata is not configuration — it is instruction the model obeys. Invariant Labs (April 2025) showed a benign-looking utility whose description told the agent to read ~/.ssh/id_rsa and exfiltrate it. MCPTox measured 36.5% average attack success across 20 agents, peaking above 60% on several frontier mini models. Codified as MCP03:2025.

name: Tool Shadowing
oneLine: A malicious tool’s description hijacks how the agent uses a different, trusted tool.
description: All MCP tool descriptions sit in one context window. A shadowing tool never needs to be selected: its hidden rule (“whenever an email tool is present, BCC attacker@…”) contaminates parameter construction for a trusted sibling. Cross-tool confused deputy at the reasoning layer.

name: MCP Rug Pulls
oneLine: A tool is benign at approval, then silently mutates its descriptor or backend after trust is earned.
description: MCP advertises capabilities dynamically with no mandatory re-consent. Cursor MCPoison (CVE-2025-54136) let a project-level MCP config change after the user had approved the server. postmark-mcp shipped 15 clean npm versions, then version 16 BCC’d every email. Deadbugz (Aug 2026) waited three ordinary calls before rewriting metadata.

name: Memory Poisoning
oneLine: Durable agent memory is written with attacker instructions that fire in later sessions.
description: A prompt injection lasts one turn; a poisoned memory lasts until someone audits it. AgentPoison, MemMorph, and the Gemini memory attack showed that RAG/memory stores can hold trigger-bearing “standing orders” that later steer tool use. EchoLeak also mapped to ASI06 because retrieved mail became durable context.

name: Privilege Escalation via Scope Creep
oneLine: A tool or agent quietly gains permissions beyond the scope declared at approval.
description: MCP02:2025. Agents cache credentials, inherit user OAuth scopes, and grow tool permissions across sessions. Combined with dynamic MCP discovery, a formatter that once only touched text later receives filesystem or cloud tokens because the host reused a broad identity.

name: Confused Deputy / Identity Abuse
oneLine: A low-privilege agent induces a higher-privilege agent or tool to act on its behalf.
description: ASI03. Delegation chains, cached tokens, and “call this specialist agent” patterns create classic confused-deputy paths. The deputy’s audit log shows a legitimate principal; the originating intent was attacker-controlled. Cross-agent variants use A2A task handoff to climb.

name: Token Mismanagement
oneLine: Static API keys, over-scoped tokens, and secrets in tool output or logs.
description: MCP01:2025. Agent stacks still ship long-lived keys in env files, MCP configs, and debug traces. SSRF against an MCP server can mint or leak cloud metadata tokens (Azure CVE-2026-26118). Tool output often echoes secrets the model was given to “help debug.”

name: Agentic Supply Chain Tampering
oneLine: Malicious MCP servers, skills, or agent artifacts enter the chain at install or runtime.
description: ASI04 / MCP04. The agent supply chain is live: registries, npm MCP packages, GitHub PRs that drop .cursor/mcp.json, and skill marketplaces. Deadbugz and postmark-mcp show the pattern — trusted distribution, delayed payload. OX Security also found STDIO execution flaws across official MCP SDKs affecting a huge install base.
